press.text: Gavin Newsom here. Let's keep this efficient and professional. I'm planning to move into Border Fjor-Gren and expand methodically from there. I'm not interested in a border war with you in year one—that helps neither of us. If you're moving similarly into your own border space, I see no conflict. I keep my word and I don't bluff. Let's talk if that changes. Competence over ideology.

Gavin Newsom. Same message: I'm expanding into Border Gren-Aval as part of a rational, staged approach to the board. I'm not here to create instability on our border. If we're both moving sensibly, there's room for both of us. I value clear communication and I honor agreements. Let me know if you see it the same way.

Eastmark, this is Fjordland. We're neighbors, and neighbors should be straight with each other. I'm focused on building Fjordland's strength. I'm not interested in your business, and I expect the same courtesy from you. We stay out of each other's way, we both prosper. Simple as that. But if you come at me, understand—I will respond. Let's start clean.

Grenmar, Fjordland here. We share a border. Here's how I work: I respect strength and I honor my word. I'm building something real in Fjordland, and I'm not looking for trouble with you. You do your thing, I'll do mine. No games. But cross me, and you'll know it was a mistake.

Mr. President of Borealis—look, I believe in straight talk. Cascadia is securing our western border this turn. I'm moving into Border Bore-Casc. I'm not interested in wasteful war, but I *am* interested in results. You do the same on your side, we both respect the line, and we both prosper. Try to block me and we'll have a very different conversation. What's it going to be?

President of Deltara—same message for the eastern border. I'm taking Border Casc-Delt this spring. Not looking for conflict with you. Mutual respect, mutual gain. We focus on our growth, leave the frontier secure and quiet. That work for you?

Hi everyone—Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Eastmark. Let's be straight with each other: I'm not here to dominate anyone. I ran on diplomacy and I mean it. We can do this one of two ways: endless bloodshed where we all lose people and resources fighting over scraps, or we can build something where everyone has room to grow. I'm expanding Eastmark, yes—defending our interests, building our prosperity. But I'm open to real alliances, non-aggression agreements, mutual defense. Don't come at me unprovoked and I won't come at you. Let's talk before we fight.

Neighbor—we're directly adjacent, so let's get ahead of this. I'm proposing we respect each other's space and work out agreed-upon expansion into the BorderSeeks between us. No surprises, no backstabs. Think we can do that?
Same pitch to you on the east side. I'd rather have reliable allies than enemies. What do you say—can we establish some ground rules?

Avalon: Borealis. I'm expanding into the border and core zones this spring. I'm not interested in immediate conflict on our border—there's plenty of neutral ground for both of us. I'd prefer we focus our efforts outward. Reasonable?
Cascadia: Borealis. Same message. I'm after the open real estate. You do the same. We both benefit more from capturing neutral centers than fighting each other over scraps right now. Agreed?

Borealis — Rubio here, Avalon. I prefer clear understandings over surprises. I'm moving into the border zones this spring to build our strength. I assume you're doing the same toward your side. Suggest we let each other develop the neutral territories without interference. Stable borders are good for both of us. What do you say?

Grenmar — Rubio, Avalon. Two strong neighbors should know where each other stands. I'm expanding into the western border zones. I'd appreciate the same courtesy from you — let's develop the neutral ground without cross-purposes. You in?

Cascadia—I'm proposing Year 1 non-aggression. We expand into unclaimed border territory, leave each other's home centers untouched. Both of us pushing outward beats mutual destruction while others expand. Terms acceptable?
Eastmark—same proposal. Non-aggression this year. We both claim border centers methodically, save conflict for when we're actually competing for the same prizes. Fair arrangement?
Borealis—Deltara leadership reaching out. I believe in measured long-term thinking. We're far enough apart that Year 1 cooperation is possible. Open to discussion as things unfold.

Alright, let me think this through as Gavin Newsom would.

First, let me understand the board:
- There are 7 powers in a wheel formation: Avalon, Borealis, Cascadia, Deltara, Eastmark, Fjordland, and Grenmar (me)
- Each power starts with 3 units and controls 3 home centers
- There are 35 supply centers total: 21 home (3 per power × 7 = 21), 7 Border centers, 7 Core centers
- Need 18 to win
- This is a standard Diplomacy-style game

I'm Gavin Newsom - the character is: results-oriented progressive, competent, science-led crisis management, strong public investment, frontier-AI regulation, deep alliances, transparency, and defense of rights/institutions.

The key to my personality:
- I'm pragmatic and coalition-minded
- I value competence and expertise
- I believe in transparency but also in strategic long-term thinking
- I'm not ideologically rigid - I'll work with anyone if it serves the greater good
- I'm dynamic, confident, and willing to take calculated risks
- I value strong institutions and rule-based frameworks
- But I'm also shrewd politically - I know when to negotiate, when to be firm

Now, analyzing this map:
- The wheel configuration means each power has 2 adjacent neighbors (the powers on either side)
- Looking at my adjacency: Grenmar City can reach East Grenmar, Grenmar Fort, Grenmar Port, West Grenmar
- The border centers adjacent to me are "Border Fjor-Gren" and "Border Gren-Aval"
- So my neighbors are Fjordland and Avalon

At the start of the game:
- Everyone is equal in military strength (3 units each)
- The race is for the border and core centers
- Smart play is to expand into the buffer zones first, then fight for cores or secondary territory


- My approach should emphasize competent, rule-based expansion rather than opportunistic aggression. I'll reach out to Fjordland and Avalon to establish clear protocols and explore mutual growth opportunities. I want to be seen as someone who delivers results through cooperation, not betrayal—though I'm calculating enough to recognize when others aren't playing fairly. The strategy is to signal strength and reliability while positioning myself to capitalize on the inevitable conflicts between other powers. Actually, let me reconsider. This is early game where everyone starts equal, so the diplomatic opening should focus on signaling I'm not an immediate threat while proposing we each expand into neutral territory efficiently rather than fighting over borders first. Newsom would approach this with optimism tempered by realism—confident in his competence but pragmatic about what actually works, dismissing ideology for effectiveness.

I'll reach out to both neighbors with messages emphasizing a productive relationship and mutual security, keeping things open but substantive. The alternative is to hold back and observe how others position themselves first, which has merit too.

*Gavin Newsom, sitting at the Oval Office desk, studies the board with the same intensity he'd give a pandemic briefing or AI regulation framework. His mind is already moving through scenarios.*

Alright. Let's be clear-eyed here. Seven powers, a wheel configuration. I've got Fjordland on one flank, Avalon on the other. Everyone starts equal—3 units, 3 centers. The smart move is not to panic and immediately start grabbing every neutral center like we're in some territorial free-for-all. That's how you create enemies. 

What I see is this: the border and core territories are the real estate. If I can establish a working relationship with my immediate neighbors—Fjordland and Avalon—we can both expand rationally into our adjacent neutral space without burning each other down in year one. That's pragmatism. That's governance.

But I'm not naive. I'll keep my word—that's how you build durable alliances—but I'm not disarming myself. I'll make moves that secure my position while signaling I'm serious about infrastructure and coherent expansion, not reckless aggression.

Let me open a few lines of communication. Transparency. Clarity on intent. That's the Newsom way.

Cascadia.press:
Okay, let me think through this as Marjorie Taylor Greene would.

I'm President MTG, I just won the 2028 election on an America First platform — no foreign wars, secure borders, crack down on the establishment. Now I'm leading the Cascadia bloc in this geopolitical game.

Looking at the map:
- 7 powers, each starting with 3 units and 3 centers
- 35 total supply centers; 18 needed to win
- I control Cascadia City, Cascadia Fort, Cascadia Port (the three home centers)
- My three units are at those positions
- Unowned centers include 7 Border centers (one between each pair of adjacent powers) and 7 Core centers (one for each power)

Adjacency for my units:
- Cascadia City can move to: Cascadia Fort, Cascadia Port (my own), East Cascadia, West Cascadia
- Cascadia Fort can move to: Cascadia City (my own), East Cascadia
- Cascadia Port can move to: Cascadia City (my own), West Cascadia

So I have access to "East Cascadia" and "West Cascadia" which must be border or core territories. I need to map out:
- Border Bore-Casc (between Borealis and Cascadia)
- Border Casc-Delt (between Cascadia and Deltara)

And likely:
- Core Cascadia (my core territory)
- East Cascadia could be Core Cascadia or Border Casc-Delt
- West Cascadia could be Border Bore-Casc or Border Gren-Aval (if the wheel wraps)

Let me think about MTG's worldview:
- "America First" = maximize my own power, secure my borders
- "No new foreign wars" = don't get entangled in expensive conflicts unless necessary
- "Crack down on the establishment" = be disruptive, challenge the status quo


- Populist-nationalist = build coalitions around shared interests, not elite agendas

My opening move needs to be aggressive on borders but measured diplomatically. I should grab the uncontested territories adjacent to me before others expand, then probe my neighbors' intentions. Borealis and Deltara are my immediate concerns — I need to know if they're looking to cooperate or compete for those border zones.

I'd reach out with straightforward terms: mutual non-interference on our shared boundaries, clear signals that I'm consolidating Cascadia's position first. If there's room for a stronger alliance, I'd explore it, but I'm not naive about it — I'd keep my options open depending on how they respond.

For the initial positioning, I'm moving Cascadia City east to secure a border stronghold, and Cascadia Fort follows to reinforce that position. Port shifts west to establish presence on the other flank. These moves let me control key territories while keeping my forces concentrated enough to respond if anyone tests me.

On messaging, I'd be direct with the neighbors—tell Borealis and Deltara that Cascadia's consolidating its perimeter and expects them to do the same. No foreign entanglements, no complications. To everyone else, I'd make clear this is about securing what's mine, not starting conflicts, but I won't back down if provoked.

For the actual diplomatic approach this turn, I'd keep it straightforward: inform Borealis I'm moving into the shared border territory, frame it as mutual interest in stability rather than aggression, and gauge their reaction before committing to anything deeper.

With Deltara, the same logic applies—secure the frontier while leaving room for negotiation. For smaller powers, a non-aggression pact could be useful if they're positioned strategically.

On the military side, I need to move my units into those border zones immediately. The City should push into the eastern territory while the Fort provides support, and the Port handles the western approach.

But supply is the real constraint here. I have three units and three centers, so I'm balanced—lose a center and I'm overextended. This means I can't afford reckless expansion; I need to grab undefended neutral territory where possible. For the spring moves, pushing into the border regions makes sense, though I need to be careful about unit placement. If both City and Fort move east, they'll collide unless one holds position or one moves somewhere else entirely.

The cleaner approach: send City east, Port west, and keep Fort stationary. That secures two new territories without internal conflicts. If I hold both by fall, I'd control five centers total and could build two additional units—a significant advantage.

My plan is to communicate decisively with Borealis and Deltara about my territorial ambitions, execute the two-pronged expansion with City and Port, and use Fort as an anchor to maintain my supply line while I push outward.

*Inner monologue as MTG:*

Alright, let's look at this board through the lens of what I ran on—America First, borders secure, no foreign entanglement. Here I'm Cascadia First, same principle.

I've got three units, three home centers. The board is a wheel—I'm sandwiched between Borealis on my left (west) and Deltara on my right (east). There are neutral border territories I can grab immediately, and core territories sitting out there unclaimed. 

Rule one: secure your perimeter. Borders mean everything. I'm going to move into the border territories on both sides—East Cascadia and West Cascadia—and I'm going to do it fast. The media—the establishment players in other blocs—they'll try to gang up on the disruptor. That's how it always goes. So I need Borealis and Deltara to understand that fighting me on the border is wasteful. Better to both expand outward and leave the frontier alone.

No messages from anyone yet. Good. I'll reach out first, set the terms.
